The man who has borne it hollowly is saved not by his own bearing but by Christ’s — the One who said “I AM” and meant every syllable — and is taught by the Spirit to mean it at last.

stations.verse: For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!
note: This is how the hollow man’s words get filled again. When a man’s own prayers have gone empty, the Spirit within him cries “Abba, Father” — filling the Name with weight from the inside. The third commandment is not finally kept by a man working up sincerity. It is kept as the Spirit of the Son prays through him, meaning “Father” with the full weight Christ always meant it, until the man’s own heart is drawn back into the reality his lips had vacated.
stations.question: Where have your own words to God gone empty — and can you let the Spirit’s cry of “Abba” fill them, rather than manufacturing sincerity yourself? What would it mean to trust the Spirit to mean it in you?
stations.gloss: to cry out, to call aloud, to shout with urgency
stations.live: When your prayers go hollow this week, stop trying to work up feeling. Pray only one word — “Father” — and trust the Spirit to cry it in you.
body: Not a mumbled formality but a cry from the depths. The Spirit does not whisper “Father” faintly in a man; He krazō — cries it out — with the full, meant weight the hollow man had lost. When your own words to God have gone hollow, the Spirit cries ‘Father’ in you with all the weight you had lost. The dust empties a man’s prayers until “Father” is a hollow sound. The Spirit krazōs it from within — crying it with meaning — refilling the Name in a man’s own mouth, so the third commandment is kept not by his effort but by the Son’s Spirit praying truly through him.

practices.title: NAME THE HOLLOW WORDS
practices.body: Write down two or three religious things you say or do on autopilot — a rote prayer, a reflexive “God is good,” a bowed head that means nothing. Do not force feeling. Just confess honestly: “Lord, I have borne Your Name here emptily.” Naming the hollowness is the first step out of it.

practices.title: PRAY ONE PRAYER YOU MEAN
practices.body: Once a day this week, pray a single short prayer slowly enough to actually mean every word — even if it is one sentence. Better one weighty sentence than a page of hollow ones. Let “Father” carry its real weight in your mouth again. Quality of meaning over quantity of words.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT CRY ABBA
practices.body: When your words go empty this week — and they will — do not manufacture sincerity. Sit in silence and pray: “Spirit, cry ‘Father’ in me; mean it where I cannot.” Trust Romans 8:15 that the Spirit fills the Name from the inside. Practice depending on His crying, not your working-up.

practices.title: PRAY THE FIRST PETITION
practices.body: Each morning this week pray Matthew 6:9 — “Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy” — and add one specific place in your day where you want His name honored: a meeting, a conversation, a hard task. Ask Him to keep His name holy there, through you.

practices.title: CLEAN UP ONE HABIT OF SPEECH
practices.body: Listen to yourself for a day. Where does God’s name slip out as filler, a curse, or a punch line? Do not white-knuckle it. Confess it, and each time it slips, replace it with a short honest word to Him.

title: His Name, Not Misused
subtitle: the Name too weighty to waste — and the One who bore it perfectly
keyVerse: You shall not misuse the name of Yahweh your God, for Yahweh will not hold him guiltless who misuses his name.

passage.text: “You shall not misuse the name of Yahweh your God, for Yahweh will not hold him guiltless who misuses his name.
Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’

stationsIntro: The verses below move through the third commandment and out to the Scriptures that expose hollow religion and reveal the Christ who bore the Name in full — the weight of God’s name, the warning against empty worship, the “Lord, Lord” that does not save, the Name revealed at the bush, and the Spirit who makes your words to God real again. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread leads from the dust of your empty religion to the Christ who kept the Name holy.
lifeIntro: This week is about finding the hollow places in your religion and letting Christ and His Spirit fill them again. The point is not to force sincerity, but to face the emptiness honestly and let the Name be made weighty in you once more. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Father, I have carried Your name like an empty sack. I said Your name with my mouth while my heart was elsewhere. I prayed words I did not mean and called it worship. Thank You that Christ never once bore Your name emptily. Let His Spirit cry “Father” in me when my words go hollow. May Your name be kept holy in me today. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have carried Your name like an empty sack.
I said Your name with my mouth while my heart was elsewhere.

Amen.
bottomLine: Misusing God’s name is not mainly cursing in the parking lot. It is bearing the weightiest Name there is over a life that empties it — prayers you don’t mean, a faith you don’t live. Christ bore the Name in full, and was given the name above every name. His Spirit now fills your hollow words with weight.
benediction: Brother, you have probably never used God’s name as a curse — and you have misused it a thousand times anyway. Every hollow prayer, every song your mouth sang while your heart wandered, every “Lord, Lord” over a life that did not follow, every religious word you emptied of its weight — that is the third commandment, broken not in the parking lot but in the pew. Because to misuse the Name is mainly this: to bear the weightiest reality in the universe while meaning nothing by it, to wear the label of God over an interior that has gone hollow.

And this is the sin hardest to see, because it hides behind a religious surface no one questions. The man who bears the Name emptily looks fine, sounds right, and clings to dust underneath. But hear the gospel: where you have emptied the Name, Christ filled it. He bore the Father’s name with perfect weight every day, said “Father” and meant the whole of it, hallowed the Name to the death — and was given the Name above every name. That Name is now the one you are saved by, not because your religion was full, but because His was. And His Spirit cries “Abba” from your chest when your own words have gone empty, filling the Name with weight from the inside.

So when you catch your worship gone hollow — and you will — lift up your eyes. Lift them off the emptiness of your own religious words and onto the Christ who never spoke one hollow word to His Father. Lift them off the gap between the Name you bear and the life you live and onto the One who closed it in your place. Lift them off your inability to mean your prayers and onto the Spirit who means “Father” in you when you cannot.

You do not have to work up a full heart to be revived. You have to bring your hollow one to the Christ who bore the Name in full, and let His Spirit fill your emptied words with weight again. The third commandment exposes the hollow man — and hands him to the One who hallowed the Name perfectly, and now teaches him to mean it.
closingVerse: You emptied the Name a thousand times. Christ filled it perfectly and was given the Name above every name — and His Spirit cries ‘Father’ in you when your own words go hollow.
carry: Where is the gap widest between the Name you bear and the life you live?

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Soul Dust to Revival
pulls: The Sabbath is a weekly confession that the world runs without you. That is why the striving man breaks it — he cannot bear to not be needed.
paras: The fourth commandment is the longest of the ten, and the one modern men break most cheerfully. Rest one day in seven — stop working, stop producing, stop striving — because God Himself rested after creation, and He made you to run on the same rhythm. It sounds gentle, even indulgent. But look at how you actually live and you will see it is the commandment you resist hardest, because it strikes at the thing you trust most: your own effort.

Underneath the Sabbath is a claim that offends the striving man to his core: the world runs without you. For one day, you lay down the tools, stop managing the universe, and let it be held by God instead of by your hands — and it does not fall apart. That is not merely a break. It is a weekly confession that you are not God, that your labor is not what holds your life together, that you can stop and the sky will not fall. The workaholic, the anxious provider, the man who cannot sit still because stillness feels like danger — the Sabbath terrifies them all, because it asks them to trust Someone other than themselves for a day.

And no striving man keeps it — not really. Even your rest is restless; even your days off are spent managing, scrolling, producing. Which is why this commandment, too, drives you to Christ: the Lord of the Sabbath, who did not merely keep the day but is the rest it always pointed to — and who says to every exhausted, striving man, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.”

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Why This Command
paras: This week goes after the striving that will not stop, and the rest that Christ Himself is. You may never once have obeyed the fourth commandment in spirit, even on the weeks you were technically off, because you cannot lay your effort down. Your identity is welded to your productivity; to stop working feels like ceasing to exist, and stillness feels like a threat. The Sabbath exposes that bondage — the inability to rest is the tell of a man trusting his own hands to hold his world.

The goal this week is to let the Sabbath expose your restless self-reliance, and to lift your eyes to Christ, who is your rest. Every road runs to Christ, and this one runs to Him as the Lord of the Sabbath and the fulfillment of it — the One in whom a man ceases from his own works, as God did from His, and finds the striving finally over.
The gospel is a Sabbath: not “work harder to be accepted” but “the work is finished; enter the rest.” And the Spirit is the one who teaches an exhausted man to stop.

Because a man’s inability to rest reveals what he actually trusts. Tell a man to stop working — truly stop, lay it all down for a day — and watch what rises: the anxiety, the twitch to check, the guilt, the sense that things will unravel without him. That reaction is a confession. It says his security rests on his own effort, that deep down he believes the world is held up by his hands. The fourth commandment matters because it goes straight to that lie. It is a weekly training in trust — a repeated, embodied rehearsal of the truth that God holds what a man cannot, that grace, not grind, is the ground he stands on. A man who cannot Sabbath cannot rest in the gospel either, because they are the same trust.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The Tools You Cannot Put Down
pulls: You Know the Restlessness
paras: God rested on the seventh day — not because He was tired, but to establish a rhythm and to declare His work complete. And He built that rhythm into the man made in His image: six days of labor, one of rest, on repeat, forever. The Sabbath is not a reward for the productive; it is a boundary against the idolatry of production. It says: your work is real and good, but it is not ultimate, and to prove it, you will stop — regularly, deliberately — and the world will keep turning without your hand on it.

But the striving man cannot put the tools down. He may leave the office, but the office does not leave him; he is still managing, still anxious, still producing in his mind if not his hands. Ask him to truly rest and he does not know how — stillness feels like idleness, idleness feels like sin, and underneath it all is the terror that if he stops, something will fall. What he cannot see is that this inability is itself the bondage the Sabbath was meant to break. He is not free. He is owned by his own effort, driven by a taskmaster crueler than any Egyptian — the belief that he must keep producing to justify his existence. The Sabbath was given to set that man free, one day a week, until the freedom seeps into all seven.

You know your own restlessness, because you feel it the moment you try to stop. The vacation you could not enjoy because you kept checking in. The Sunday afternoon that filled up with tasks because sitting still felt wrong. The quiet evening that made you reach for your phone within ninety seconds. The guilt that rises when you are not being useful. That restlessness is not a personality trait to manage — it is a soul that has forgotten how to trust, a man who has confused his effort with his worth. The Sabbath names it. And it offers the one thing the striving man cannot give himself: permission, and power, to stop.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: The Lord of the Sabbath Is the Rest
paras: Now lift your eyes to Christ, who called Himself the Lord of the Sabbath — and meant far more than that He could decide what was lawful on the day. He is the reality the Sabbath was a shadow of. Every seventh day of rest, for every generation of Israel, was a signpost pointing forward to a Person in whom the striving would finally end. And when He came, He did not say “keep the day better.” He said something that no mere teacher could say: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.” He offered Himself as the Sabbath — the place a weary man lays his effort down for good.

The gospel goes deeper into this commandment than that. On the cross, Jesus cried “It is finished” — the ultimate Sabbath declaration. The work of saving you is done; there is nothing left for you to add. And then — do not miss this — He rested in the tomb on the Sabbath day. The Lord of the Sabbath kept a literal Sabbath in death, His saving work complete, before rising on the first day to inaugurate a new creation. The writer of Hebrews draws it out: “he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.” The gospel is a Sabbath. It is the end of striving to be accepted, because Christ has done the work. And this is the fourth commandment fulfilled: not a man white-knuckling one day off, but a man who has ceased from his own works — laid down the tools of self-justification — and entered the rest that Christ Himself is. The Spirit’s work is to walk an exhausted man into that rest, and teach his frantic hands, at last, to open.

stations.verse: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.
note: The command is grounded in creation itself. God worked, then rested — and wrote that rhythm into the world and the man. Notice the first word: remember. The Sabbath is something men forget, precisely because striving feels so urgent and stopping feels so dangerous. To keep it holy is to set one day apart as different — a day that declares, against all your anxiety, that the world is held by God and not by you.
stations.question: When did you last truly stop — laid down the work, the managing, the producing, for a full day? What rises in you at the thought of it, and what does that reaction reveal about what you are trusting?
stations.gloss: to cease, to stop, to desist
stations.live: Choose one block of hours this week and stop — no work, no managing, no phone. When the urge to produce rises, name it and let it pass. That is šāḇaṯ.
body: The root of Sabbath. It does not primarily mean to nap or relax; it means to stop — to bring the labor to a halt. At creation God did not rest because He was weary; He šāḇaṯ — ceased — to mark the work complete (Genesis 2:2). The command is not mainly ‘relax.’ It is ‘stop’ — and stopping is the very thing the striving man cannot do. The dust drives a man to labor without ceasing, as if the world depended on his hands. Šāḇaṯ is the weekly, holy stop — the ceasing that confesses God holds what the man cannot, and points to the Christ in whom a man ceases for good.

stations.verse: He said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.
note: Jesus corrects two errors at once. The Sabbath is not a burden man exists to serve — it was made for man, a gift for his good. And Jesus claims lordship over it: He is the Lord of the Sabbath, the one who defines it and, ultimately, the one who is it. The day was always for the sake of the man, and the man was always meant to find, in it, the rest that is finally a Person.
stations.question: Have you experienced the Sabbath as a burden or a gift — or ignored it entirely? How does it change things to know the Lord of the Sabbath made it for your good, and is Himself the rest it offers?
stations.gloss: lord, master, the one with authority and ownership
stations.live: Ask Christ, the Lord of the Sabbath, what He wants your day of rest to look like this week — and do the first thing He brings to mind.
body: Jesus calls Himself Kyrios of the Sabbath — not its breaker, but its owner and its meaning. The One who has authority over the day is the One the day was always pointing toward. The Sabbath was never your master. Its Master is Christ — and He made the day to lead you to Himself. The dust turns the Sabbath into either a rule to resent or a gift to ignore. Kyrios reframes it: the day belongs to Christ, was made for the man’s good, and finds its whole meaning in the rest He gives.

stations.verse: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
note: This is the Sabbath offered as a Person. Jesus does not say “keep the day and you will find rest.” He says come to Me. The weary and heavily burdened — the striving man, the anxious provider, the one who cannot put the tools down — are invited not to a better technique but to a Person who gives what the day only pictured. The rest is not scheduled; it is received, from Christ, by coming.
stations.question: What are you laboring under and burdened with right now — the weight you carry that will not let you rest? What would it mean this week to actually come to Christ with it, rather than managing it alone?
stations.gloss: to give rest, to refresh, to cause to cease from labor
stations.live: Name the single heaviest weight you are carrying. Once a day this week, take it to Christ in prayer by name, and leave it with Him before you get up.
body: The word for relief given to the exhausted — the unyoking of a worn animal, the refreshment of a spent man. Jesus promises to anapauō the weary — to be their ceasing. You cannot schedule the rest your soul needs. You can only come to the One who gives it. The dust leaves a man laboring and heavily burdened, unable to rest himself. Anapauō is the rest Christ gives — not earned, not manufactured, but received by the man who finally stops striving and comes.

stations.verse: Therefore the children of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, to observe the Sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant. It is a sign between me and the children of Israel forever; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed.’
note: Yahweh gives the Sabbath as a sign, and then grounds it in a staggering sentence about Himself: “on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed.” God was not tired. But He stopped, and He took His breath, and He called it good. The Sabbath is a man stepping into that same breath — confessing every week that the world was finished by Another and is held by Another. And on the cross, Christ cried “It is finished” over the work of your salvation, and rested in the tomb on the Sabbath day. The work is done. Breathe.
stations.question: When did you last stop long enough to catch your breath — not to recover so you could produce more, but to rest in what God has finished? What keeps you from it?
stations.gloss: to take breath, to refresh oneself
stations.live: Once a day this week, stop for two minutes, breathe slowly, and say: “It is finished. I can stop.” Let your body learn what your soul already knows.
body: A rare verb — used of weary servants and strangers getting their breath back on the Sabbath, of a king and his men refreshed after a hard road, and here of God Himself on the seventh day. It is related to nep̄eš, the breath-soul of a living thing. God took His breath on the seventh day. The Sabbath invites you to take yours in His finished work. The dust drives a man until he has no breath left, as if the world depended on his lungs. Nāp̄aš is God’s own exhale over a finished creation — and the Sabbath is the man breathing with Him, resting in the work Christ finished on the cross.

stations.verse: There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God. For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.
note: Hebrews reveals what the weekly Sabbath was always pointing to: a deeper rest, entered by faith in Christ, where a man rests from his own works as God rested from His. This is the fourth commandment fulfilled — not merely a day off, but the end of self-salvation, the laying down of every effort to justify oneself. The rest remains, still on offer, for every striving man who will cease from his own works and trust the finished work of Christ.
stations.question: Have you entered the deeper Sabbath — resting from your own works of self-justification — or are you still laboring to establish your own standing? Where do you most need to “rest from your works” this week?
stations.gloss: a Sabbath-keeping, a Sabbath rest; built on the verb for keeping the Sabbath, and used in the New Testament only here, for the deeper rest the weekly Sabbath foreshadowed
stations.live: Write down the one thing you are still working to earn — approval, security, a sense of being enough. Under it write Hebrews 4:10, and read it back each night this week.
body: It is not merely stopping for a day but the settled, ongoing rest of a soul that has ceased striving to save itself and rests in Christ’s finished work. There remains a rest deeper than a day off — the soul’s ceasing from its own works, entered by faith in Christ. The dust is a man who never enters the sabbatismos — who keeps laboring to justify himself, restless in his soul even on his days off. The gospel opens the true rest: cease from your own works, trust the finished work of Christ, and enter the Sabbath that remains.

practices.title: TRY TO STOP, AND WATCH WHAT RISES
practices.body: Set aside a few hours — or a full day if you can — and deliberately stop: no work, no managing, no producing. Then notice what rises: anxiety, guilt, the twitch to check. Do not suppress it. Name it: “This restlessness is showing me what I trust.” Let the inability to rest expose the striving underneath.

practices.title: PREACH ‘IT IS FINISHED’ TO YOUR STRIVING
practices.body: Name the one thing you are most striving to earn — approval, security, a sense of being enough. This week, each time you feel the striving, say over it: “It is finished. Christ has done the work. I can stop.” Practice hearing the Sabbath word of the gospel over the effort you cannot lay down.

practices.title: COME, DON’T JUST REST
practices.body: Instead of only scheduling rest, practice coming to the Person. When you are weary this week, pray Matthew 11:28 as an actual coming: “Lord, I am laboring and heavily burdened. I come to You. Give me rest.” Depend on Christ to be your Sabbath, not just the calendar.

practices.title: KEEP ONE REAL DAY
practices.body: Plan your Lord’s Day this week before it comes. Decide what you will not do — work email, chores, errands — and what you will do: worship with God’s people, eat a slow meal, take a walk, sleep. Treat it as a gift to receive, not a rule to pass.

practices.title: WATCH CHRIST ON THE SABBATH
practices.body: Read Mark 2:23–3:6. Watch what Jesus does on the Sabbath: He feeds the hungry and heals a withered hand. Ask Him what restful mercy you could do on your day of rest — and do it.

title: Remember the Sabbath
subtitle: the rest we could not keep — and the Lord of the Sabbath who is our rest
keyVerse: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work…

passage.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
You shall labor six days, and do all your work,

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates;
for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.
He was going on the Sabbath day through the grain fields, and his disciples began, as they went, to pluck the ears of grain.
The Pharisees said to him, “Behold, why do they do that which is not lawful on the Sabbath day?”
He said to them, “Did you never read what David did, when he had need, and was hungry—he, and those who were with him?
How he entered into God’s house at the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the show bread, which is not lawful to eat except for the priests, and gave also to those who were with him?”
He said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”

stationsIntro: The verses below move through the fourth commandment and out to the Scriptures that expose your restlessness and reveal the Christ who is your rest — the creation Sabbath, the Lord of the Sabbath, the invitation to the weary, the God who was refreshed, and the rest that remains. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread leads from the dust of your striving to the Christ in whom the striving ends.
lifeIntro: This week is about facing your restlessness and entering the rest Christ gives. The point is not to grit your way into a better day off, but to let your inability to stop reveal what you trust, and to come to Christ for the rest He is. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Father, I do not know how to stop. I hold my life up with tired hands and call it faithfulness. Even my rest is restless. Thank You that Christ said, “It is finished,” over all my striving. Teach my hands to open and my lungs to breathe. Bring me into the rest that remains. I come to You, Lord of the Sabbath. Give me rest. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I do not know how to stop.
I hold my life up with tired hands and call it faithfulness.
Even my rest is restless.
Thank You that Christ said, “It is finished,” over all my striving.
Teach my hands to open and my lungs to breathe.
Bring me into the rest that remains.
I come to You, Lord of the Sabbath. Give me rest. Amen.
bottomLine: Your inability to rest is a confession of what you trust. The Sabbath tells the truth: the world was finished by God and is held by God, not by you. Christ is the rest the day pointed to. He finished the work, and He calls every burdened man to come and stop.
benediction: Brother, the fourth commandment is the one you break most cheerfully and resist most deeply — because it asks the one thing the striving man cannot do. Stop. Lay down the tools. Let the world be held by God for a day and watch it not fall apart. And your inability to do it is a confession: that you believe, underneath, that your life is held up by your own hands, that stopping is dangerous, that you must keep producing to justify your existence. The Sabbath names that bondage. Your restlessness is the tell.

And no striving man keeps this commandment — even his rest is restless. But hear the gospel that is deeper here than in almost any command: the Lord of the Sabbath came, and He is the rest. He did not say “keep the day better.” He said, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.” He cried “It is finished” over the work of your salvation, rested in the tomb with that work complete, and rose to open a rest that remains — the soul’s ceasing from its own works, entered by faith in Him. The gospel is a Sabbath. The striving to earn God is over.

So when you find yourself unable to stop, driven, checking, guilty in the stillness — lift up your eyes. Lift them off the tools you cannot put down and onto the Christ who finished the only work that ever mattered. Lift them off the world you are trying to hold up and onto the God who holds it without your help. Lift them off your restless self-reliance and onto the Lord of the Sabbath, who says to every burdened man, “Come to me … and I will give you rest.”

You do not have to strive your way into rest to be revived. You have to come to the One who is your rest, cease from your own works as God did from His, and let His Spirit teach your frantic hands to open. The fourth commandment exposes the striving man — and hands him to the Christ in whom the striving, at last, is finished.
closingVerse: You could not lay the tools down. Christ cried ‘It is finished,’ rested in the tomb, and rose as your rest. Cease from your works. Come to the Lord of the Sabbath.
carry: What do you believe would fall apart if you truly stopped?

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Soul Dust to Revival
pulls: How a man treats the authority nearest him — the parents who gave him life — reveals his heart toward all authority, including God’s. Honor begins at home.
paras: The fifth commandment is the hinge of the ten — the first that turns from a man’s duty toward God to his duty toward people, and it starts, tellingly, at home. Before God addresses murder, adultery, theft, or lying, He addresses the family. Honor your father and your mother. Because the way a man treats the authority nearest to him — the ones who gave him life, flawed as they were — reveals the posture of his heart toward all authority, including God’s.

And this commandment is wider than a child obeying young parents. It is the only one of the ten with a promise attached — that your days may be long — and it reaches across a whole life: the adult son caring for aging parents, the man carrying the wounds of a father who failed him, the heart’s fundamental stance toward every authority God has placed over him. To honor is to assign weight, to treat as worthy of respect, to refuse the contempt and dismissal that come so easily. And here the dust rises, because most men carry, somewhere, a deep dishonor — a parent resented, a wound nursed, an authority despised.

This is a hard commandment for the wounded, and most men are wounded here. Some had fathers who were absent, harsh, or worse. Honor does not mean pretending the wounds were not real. But it does expose the contempt you have justified, the bitterness you have fed, the dishonor you have called realism. And like every command, it drives you to Christ — the perfect Son, who honored His Father with an obedience unto death, and who honored His earthly parents too, and who now, by His Spirit, can heal the dishonoring heart and even the wounds beneath it.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Why This Command
paras: This week goes after the dishonor you have justified, and the Son who honored perfectly in your place — including for the deeply wounded. A lot of men have a resented parent, a bitterness they have nursed for years, a contempt toward authority they have dressed up as independence or realism. And a lot of men were genuinely wronged, which makes the commandment feel impossible or even cruel. This week means to handle both honestly: the real wounds, and the real dishonor, without collapsing one into the other.

The goal is to let the fifth commandment expose the contempt in your heart — toward parents, and toward all authority — and to lift your eyes to Christ, the honoring Son. Every road runs to Christ, and this one runs to Him as the Son who honored His Father to the death, who honored His mother even from the cross, and whose perfect honor is credited to men whose hearts have been full of dishonor. The Spirit can do what willpower cannot: soften a hard heart, and even begin to heal the wound the dishonor grew from.

Because the family is where a man first learns whether authority can be trusted — and that lesson shapes everything, including his relationship with God. A man who despises his parents will struggle to honor any authority, and will find it hard to submit to the ultimate Authority, God Himself. The fifth commandment matters because the home is the training ground for the heart’s whole posture toward those set over a man. It is also the commandment where wounds run deepest, which makes it a place the gospel must go — not to excuse abuse or demand pretense, but to free a man from the corrosive dishonor that keeps him bound to the very people who hurt him. Honor, rightly understood, is not weakness before an abuser. It is freedom from the bitterness that would otherwise own a man for life.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Honor Is Not the Same as Agreement
pulls: You Know Your Own Dishonor
paras: The word honor trips men up, especially wounded ones, because they hear it as approval — as if to honor a parent means to pretend they were good, to endorse what they did, to submit to whatever they demand. That is not what the commandment means, and reading it that way has kept many a wounded man in needless torment. To honor is to assign weight — to treat a person as significant, to refuse contempt, to give the respect due to their place even when their conduct did not earn it. A man can honor a parent he must also confront, forgive, or keep at a distance. Honor is a posture of the heart, not a blanket endorsement of behavior.

This matters because the sin the commandment targets is contempt — the dismissing of a person as worthless, the bitterness that reduces them to their worst moments, the settled scorn a man can carry for decades. That contempt does not punish the parent nearly as much as it corrodes the son. And most men miss this: you can hold a person accountable, name real wrong, even establish hard boundaries, and still refuse contempt. The dishonor the commandment forbids is not the naming of truth about a parent’s failure. It is the scorn in the heart that dehumanizes them — and that scorn is a poison the son drinks, hoping the parent will die.

You can find your dishonor by noticing the tone in your chest when a certain parent comes to mind — the eye-roll, the old resentment, the story you have rehearsed a hundred times of how they failed you. Maybe the failure was real; many are. But notice how the story has hardened into contempt, how the bitterness has become a familiar companion you almost do not want to give up, because giving it up feels like letting them off. That is the dishonor the commandment names. Not the memory of a real wound — but the scorn you have built on top of it, and fed, until it became part of how you see. The fifth commandment does not ask you to deny the wound. It asks you to stop letting the wound curdle into contempt that is slowly hardening your whole heart.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: The Son Who Honored to the End
paras: Now lift your eyes to Christ, the perfect Son — for the fifth commandment is, at its root, about sonship, and Jesus is the Son who honored His Father flawlessly. His whole life was a honoring: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him.” He honored the Father not just when it was easy but in Gethsemane, sweating blood, when honor meant a cross — not My will but Yours. He honored the Father to the death, an obedience unto death, even death on a cross. Where every man has, somewhere, withheld honor, Christ gave it in full, all the way down.

And He honored His earthly parents too. As a boy He was subject to Joseph and Mary. And in one of the most tender moments in all of Scripture — hanging on the cross, in agony, with the weight of the world’s sin on Him — He looked down at His mother and made provision for her care, giving her to the beloved disciple: “Woman, behold, your son!” … “Behold, your mother!” Even dying, He honored His mother. This is the honor now credited to you: the perfect sonship of Christ, offered in exchange for your dishonor. When the Father looks at the man in Christ, He does not see a heart full of contempt for authority — He sees the flawless honor of His Son, reckoned to a man who withheld it. And the Spirit’s mercy goes further: He who cries “Abba, Father” in a man’s heart is remaking his whole posture toward authority — softening the contempt, and going down beneath it to touch the wound it grew from. The man who could not honor is, by the Spirit, made a son who can — and even the father-wound begins, slowly, to heal in the presence of a perfect Father.

stations.verse: Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.
note: The one command with a promise. Long life in the land — not as a magic reward, but because a society and a soul that honor authority rightly are stable, and one built on contempt corrodes from within. Honoring is life-giving; contempt is slowly fatal, first to the one who carries it. God attaches a promise here because He is pointing to a whole way of being that either builds a man up or eats him alive.
stations.question: What is the actual posture of your heart toward your parents — honor, or a contempt you have justified? Where has bitterness toward a parent been quietly corroding you more than it ever touched them?
stations.gloss: to honor, but the root literally means to be heavy, weighty
stations.live: Think of the parent you find hardest to honor. Name one true, good thing about them, and say it — to God, to them, or to someone else — before the week is out.
body: To honor someone is to assign them weight, to treat them as significant. The opposite, qālal — the word Exodus 21:17 uses for cursing a parent — means to be light, to treat as trivial. To honor is to give weight; to dishonor is to make weightless. To honor is to give a person weight. Contempt is making them weightless — and it is your own soul that grows light and hard. The dust makes a man treat a parent as weightless — dismissed, reduced to their failures. Kāḇēḏ calls him to assign weight instead, not endorsing the wrong but refusing the contempt, and points to the Son who gave His Father full weight to the death.

stations.verse: For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him be put to death.’ But you say, ‘Whoever may tell his father or his mother, “Whatever help you might otherwise have gotten from me is a gift devoted to God,” he shall not honor his father or mother.’ You have made the commandment of God void because of your tradition.
note: Jesus rebukes men who found a religious loophole to avoid caring for their aging parents — dedicating to God the money they should have used to support them. He exposes how the human heart will use even religion to dodge honor. The commandment is not abstract; it has hands and feet — the practical care of parents in their need. Dishonor often hides behind respectable excuses, and Jesus drags it into the light.
stations.question: Where have you used a respectable excuse — busyness, distance, even spirituality — to avoid the practical honor of caring for or being present to a parent? What honor are you withholding behind a justification?
stations.gloss: to honor, to value, to set a price on as precious
stations.live: Do one concrete act of honor this week that costs you something — time, money, attention — for a parent or an older person God has placed near you.
body: Related to the word for price or value. To honor a parent is to treat them as precious, to assign them real value — not in the abstract, but in the concrete provision and respect Jesus insists it includes. Honor that costs nothing and does nothing is not honor. Christ insists it has hands. The dust dresses dishonor in respectable clothes — excuses that void the command while looking pious. Timaō calls for real, costly valuing of parents, and drives the excuse-making man to the Christ who honored not in word only but unto death.

stations.verse: He who sent me is with me. The Father hasn’t left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.
note: The honoring Son describes His whole life in one line: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him.” Not sometimes, not mostly — always. This is the perfect honor no man has given: a life entirely oriented toward pleasing the Father. And it is offered to you, credited to your account, in place of the dishonor you have carried. Christ’s flawless sonship is the honor the fifth commandment demanded and you could never supply.
stations.question: Can you receive Christ’s perfect honoring of the Father as credited to you — covering the dishonor in your own heart? How does His “always pleasing” free you from having to manufacture a clean record yourself?
stations.gloss: pleasing, acceptable, satisfying
stations.live: Each night this week, before you list your failures, read John 8:29 and thank God that Christ’s “always” is counted to you.
body: What is arestos to the Father delighted Him. Jesus lived a life wholly arestos — pleasing — to God, the perfect Son honoring the perfect Father without a single lapse. Christ’s whole life was pleasing to the Father — and that flawless honor is credited to the man whose heart was full of contempt. The dust leaves a man with a record of dishonor he cannot undo. Christ’s arestos life — always pleasing to the Father — is reckoned to that man in the gospel, so his standing rests on the Son’s honor, not his own.

stations.verse: Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!” Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.
note: One of the most tender scenes in Scripture. Dying, in unimaginable agony, bearing the sin of the world, Jesus still honors His mother — arranging her care, giving her a son to look after her. Even the cross did not stop His honoring. This is the fifth commandment kept to the very last breath, under a weight no man has borne. The perfect Son honored His mother from the cross, and that honor is now the covering for your neglect.
stations.question: Christ honored His mother even while dying for the world. Where have you let your own pain or burden excuse you from honoring a parent — when His far greater pain did not excuse Him?
stations.gloss: behold! look! see! An urgent word calling for attention
stations.live: Whose care have you let your own burden excuse you from? Make one phone call, visit, or arrangement this week that says, “Behold, your mother.”
body: From the cross, Jesus says ide — behold — your son, your mother, binding two people into a family bond of care in His final moments. Even dying, His attention turned to the honoring of His mother. He was dying for the sins of the world, and He still stopped to make sure His mother would be cared for. The dust lets a man’s own suffering excuse his dishonor. Christ’s ide from the cross — behold your mother — shatters the excuse: the One in the greatest agony ever suffered still honored His mother, and covers, with that honor, the neglect of men who would not.

stations.verse: When my father and my mother forsake me, then Yahweh will take me up.
note: For the deeply wounded, this is the gospel’s tenderness. The commandment to honor does not deny that some parents forsake, fail, even abandon. But it comes with a Father who does not — Yahweh, who takes up the forsaken. A man wounded by a father or mother is not left to honor out of an empty tank; he is given a perfect Father whose love can fill what the earthly one could not, and heal the wound the dishonor grew from. Honor becomes possible when the wound is being healed by One who never forsakes.
stations.question: If you carry a wound from a parent who failed or forsook you, can you receive the Father who takes in the forsaken? How might being loved by a perfect Father begin to free you from the contempt — and heal the wound beneath it?
stations.gloss: to gather, to take in, to receive to oneself
stations.live: If a parent forsook or failed you, write Psalm 27:10 on a card and pray it daily this week as your own: “then Yahweh will take me up.”
body: The word for gathering in the harvest, or taking a wanderer into your home. When father and mother forsake, Yahweh will ʾāsap̄ — gather in, take up — the abandoned one, taking him into the family that will never cast him out. The parent may forsake. The Father gathers in — and heals the wound the forsaking left. The dust of a father-wound tempts a man to a lifelong contempt. ʾĀsap̄ offers another way: gathered in by a Father who never forsakes, the wounded man finds his emptiness filled and his heart softened — free, at last, to honor without pretending, because he is finally, fully loved.

practices.title: NAME THE CONTEMPT HONESTLY
practices.body: Write down, honestly, the contempt you carry toward a parent — the resentment, the rehearsed story, the scorn. Do not deny any real wound. But name the contempt built on top of it as its own thing: “This scorn is corroding me.” Distinguish the wound (real) from the contempt (poison you are drinking).

practices.title: RECEIVE THE SON’S HONOR AND THE FATHER’S LOVE
practices.body: This week, pray both halves: “Christ honored perfectly in my place; His record covers my dishonor,” and “Father, take me in where my parents failed.” Let the gospel address both your guilt (covered by the Son) and your wound (gathered in by the Father). Do not rush past either.

practices.title: TAKE ONE CONCRETE STEP OF HONOR
practices.body: Ask what one honoring step is possible and wise — a call, a kind word, a practical care, a boundary held without contempt. It need not mean pretending or exposing yourself to harm. It means refusing scorn and assigning weight. Take the one step the Spirit makes clear, from a heart being softened, not forced.

practices.title: HONOR THE OLDER MEN AROUND YOU
practices.body: The fifth commandment reaches past your parents to every authority God has set near you. Write a short note this week to an older man in your church or work — thanking him for something specific. Honor given freely softens the heart that gives it.

practices.title: FORGIVE ONE DEBT OUT LOUD
practices.body: If there is a parent you need to forgive, write out what they owe you — honestly. Then pray over the page: “Father, You forgave me in Christ. I release this to You.” You may still need boundaries. You do not need contempt.

title: Honor Father and Mother
subtitle: the honor we withheld — and the Son who honored His Father to death
keyVerse: Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.

passage.text: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.
But standing by Jesus’ cross were his mother, his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”
Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.

stationsIntro: The verses below move through the fifth commandment and out to the Scriptures that expose your dishonor and reveal the honoring Son — the command with a promise, the contempt God forbids, the Son who pleased His Father, the Son who cared for His mother from the cross, and the Father who heals the wound. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread leads from the dust of your contempt to the Christ who honored perfectly.
lifeIntro: This week is about facing the dishonor in your heart, receiving Christ’s perfect honoring, and letting the Father heal the wound beneath it. The point is not to pretend wounds away or force feelings, but to let contempt be named and grace go to work. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Father, I have treated people You gave me as weightless. I have nursed old wounds into contempt and called my bitterness realism. Thank You that Christ always did what pleased You, and honored His mother even from the cross. Let His honor cover my dishonor. Where my parents failed me, take me up. Soften what has gone hard in me. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have treated people You gave me as weightless.
I have nursed old wounds into contempt
and called my bitterness realism.
Thank You that Christ always did what pleased You,
and honored His mother even from the cross.
Let His honor cover my dishonor.
Where my parents failed me, take me up.
Soften what has gone hard in me. Amen.
bottomLine: To honor is to give weight. Contempt makes a person weightless — and it is your own soul that grows light and hard. Christ honored His Father to the death and His mother from the cross. His honor covers your dishonor, and the Father who takes up the forsaken heals the wound beneath it.
benediction: Brother, the fifth commandment turns the corner from God to people, and it starts at home — because how you treat the authority nearest you reveals your heart toward all authority, including God’s. Honor your father and mother. And here the dust rises in almost every man, because almost every man carries a dishonor somewhere: a parent resented, a wound nursed into contempt, a scorn he has justified as realism. Maybe the wound was real — many are. But the commandment names the contempt you built on top of it, the bitterness you have fed until it hardened your heart, the poison you keep drinking hoping the other person will die.

And no man honors perfectly — but One did. Christ, the perfect Son, honored His Father to the death, always doing what pleased Him, obedient even to the cross. And He honored His mother from that cross, in the greatest agony ever suffered, arranging her care with some of His final breaths. That flawless honor is now credited to you, covering the contempt in your heart. And more: the Father who takes in the forsaken offers to gather you in, to fill what your parents could not, and to heal the very wound your dishonor grew from.

So when the old contempt rises — and it will — lift up your eyes. Lift them off the parent you have reduced to their failures and onto the Son who honored His Father in full for you. Lift them off the bitterness corroding you and onto the Christ whose perfect record covers your dishonor. Lift them off the wound you have carried alone and onto the Father who takes in the forsaken and never casts them out.

You do not have to manufacture honor from an empty, wounded tank to be revived. You have to receive the Son’s honor as your covering and the Father’s love as your healing, and let the Spirit soften the contempt from the inside. The fifth commandment exposes the dishonoring heart — and hands the wounded man to a perfect Father and a perfect Son, who together can make him, at last, a son who honors.
closingVerse: You withheld honor; Christ gave it to the death, and to His mother from the cross. His honor covers your contempt — and the Father who takes in the forsaken heals the wound beneath it.
carry: Whose name makes something tighten in your chest — and what would giving them weight look like?

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Soul Dust to Revival
pulls: Behind every murder is anger. Jesus traces the act to its root and finds the root in you — the contempt that wishes a man gone. The commandment for killers is a commandment for everyone.
paras: The sixth commandment is two words in Hebrew, and most men read it and relax. You shall not murder — well, I haven’t killed anyone, so this one’s covered. And then Jesus takes those two words and drives them straight into the chest of every man alive. “You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ … But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment.” He traces the act back to its root, and the root is in you.

This is the pattern of the whole Sermon on the Mount, and it is the pattern of how the Law drives a man to Christ. The commandment does not merely forbid the outward deed; it exposes the inner disposition the deed grows from. Behind murder is hatred. Behind the act is the anger that wishes a man gone, the contempt that dismisses him as worthless, the resentment nursed until it curdles into a quiet death-wish. Jesus says the man who has felt that has already broken the sixth commandment in his heart. Suddenly the commandment for murderers is a commandment for everyone.

And that is its mercy. Because if the sixth commandment only condemned the man who pulled a trigger, every other man would use it to feel righteous while his heart stayed full of contempt. Jesus will not allow it. He exposes the murder in the ordinary man’s anger, stops his self-righteous mouth, and drives him to the only One who is truly innocent of it — the Christ who not only never murdered but never hated, and who let His own life be taken so that men full of death could live.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Why This Command
paras: This week goes after the anger and contempt you have excused, and the Christ who gave His life for men full of death. A lot of men read “do not murder” and feel safe, while carrying grudges, contempt, and a low-grade hatred toward people who have wronged them — all of which Jesus calls murder of the heart. This week means to take the commandment as deep as He took it, past the hands and into the disposition.

The goal is to let the sixth commandment expose the death-wish hiding in ordinary anger, and to lift your eyes to the Christ who is both perfectly innocent of it and the sacrifice for it. Every road runs to Christ, and this one runs to Him two ways: as the One who never hated, whose perfect love is credited to the hateful, and as the Life that was taken — the innocent murdered so that the guilty could go free. The commandment against killing is answered by a killing: the death of the Prince of life, for men who deserved death.

Because human life bears the image of God, and to attack it — in deed or in the heart — is to attack the God whose image it carries. That is why murder is so grave: not merely that it ends a life, but that it defaces an image-bearer of God. And that is why Jesus can trace it into the heart: the contempt that dismisses a person as worthless, the anger that wishes them gone, is already a denial of the image of God in them. The sixth commandment matters because it guards the sacred worth of persons all the way down to the attitude of the heart. A man who harbors contempt has not kept the commandment just because his hands are clean. He has broken it where it starts.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Murder Starts Long Before the Hands
pulls: You Know the Contempt
paras: Jesus does surgery on this commandment, and the incision is deep. He takes murder back to its source and names three stages on the road: the anger that smolders, the contempt that dismisses (“you fool”), and the settled hatred that would be glad to see a man gone. All three, He says, fall under the sixth commandment’s judgment, because all three are murder in seed form. The outward act is only the flower; the root is in the heart, and the root is where the commandment reaches.

This is devastating for the respectable man, and it is meant to be. The man who would never lift a hand can carry, for years, a quiet contempt for a brother, an ex-friend, an enemy at work — rehearsing their faults, savoring their failures, wishing them diminished. He tells himself he would never actually harm them, and he is right about his hands. But Jesus is asking about his heart, and in the heart the death-wish is doing its slow work — not killing the other man, but killing something in the one who carries it. Contempt is a low-grade murder a man commits mostly against his own soul, and the sixth commandment names it for what it is.

You know your own version, because a face probably came to mind already. The person you have written off. The one whose downfall you would quietly enjoy. The enemy you have rehearsed arguments against in the shower. The family member you have reduced, in your mind, to their worst quality. You would never harm them — but you have wished them smaller, gladly imagined their comeuppance, felt the little flare of satisfaction at their trouble. Jesus calls that the seed of murder. Not because you are about to kill anyone, but because contempt is the disposition murder grows from, and He will not let you feel innocent while it lives in you. The commandment you thought you had kept turns out to have your name on it.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: The Life Taken So the Guilty Could Live
paras: Now lift your eyes to Christ, who answers this commandment in a way that goes to the very bottom of the gospel. First, He is the only man who kept it perfectly — not just in deed but in disposition. He never hated. Even toward His murderers, His word was “Father, forgive them.” The contempt that fills every other human heart was entirely absent from His. That flawless, love-filled heart is now credited to men whose hearts have been full of the death-wish — the perfect innocence of Christ covering the murder you committed in your anger.

But the gospel goes further and darker here. The commandment against murder was answered by a murder. The Prince of life — the innocent Son, guilty of no anger, no contempt, no death-wish — was taken by wicked hands and killed. Peter says it plainly: you “killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead.” The sinless One was murdered so that the murderers could live. This is the deep exchange at the heart of the sixth commandment: the innocent Life was taken so that the guilty could go free. Every man who has harbored the murder of contempt is a man for whom the innocent Christ died — and in His death, the death-sentence the commandment pronounced over the hateful heart falls on Him instead. And His Spirit, poured into a man, begins to drain the contempt out and replace it with the very love Christ had for His enemies — so that the man who carried a death-wish learns, slowly, to wish his enemy life.

stations.verse: Whoever sheds man’s blood, his blood will be shed by man, for God made man in his own image.
note: Murder is grave because man bears the image of God. To attack a person is to attack the image of the One who made them. This is the foundation under the sixth commandment — and the reason Jesus can extend it to contempt. To dismiss a person as worthless, to wish them gone, is to deny the image of God stamped on them. The commandment guards not just life but the sacred dignity of every image-bearer.
stations.question: Who have you been treating as less than an image-bearer of God — dismissed, reduced, written off? How does remembering the image of God in them confront the contempt you have carried?
stations.gloss: to pour out, to spill, to shed
stations.live: Think of the person you have written off. Pray Psalm 62:8 this week: pour out your heart about them to God, honestly — and ask Him to show you His image in them.
body: The verb for pouring water on the ground, pouring out a drink offering, pouring out wrath — and, in Genesis 9:6, shedding a man’s blood. Blood poured on the ground cannot be gathered back. The reason God gives for guarding it is in the same verse: “God made man in his own image” — the ṣelem of God. The person you hold in contempt bears the image of God. Your scorn is poured out on His likeness. The dust lets a man reduce his enemy to something less than an image-bearer, and contempt pours out what it can never gather back. Šāp̄aḵ names the spilling — and points ahead to the One whose blood was poured out for the many, so that men full of death could live.

stations.verse: You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’ But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna.
note: Here Jesus drives the commandment into the heart. Anger, contempt, the dismissive “fool” — all of it falls under the sixth commandment’s judgment, because all of it is murder in seed. He refuses to let the man with clean hands feel innocent while his heart is full of the death-wish. This is the Law doing its deepest work: stopping the self-righteous mouth of the respectable man and showing him the murderer within.
stations.question: Whose face came to mind when you read “angry with his brother”? Where have you felt innocent of this commandment while carrying anger and contempt that Jesus calls its violation?
stations.gloss: liable to, held in, bound under a sentence
stations.live: Name the grudge you are keeping warm. Before the week is out, take one step toward reconciling — a call, an apology, a prayer for that man by name (Matthew 5:23–24).
body: A legal word — a man “held in” by a charge, answerable to a court. Jesus uses it four times in Matthew 5:21–22: the murderer is enochos to the judgment, and so is the man angry with his brother without a cause, and so is the man who calls him a fool. The anger Jesus calls murder is not the flash that passes. It is the grudge you keep warm — and it holds you liable. The dust tells the angry man he is innocent because his hands are clean. Enochos says otherwise: the harbored grudge already stands under sentence. And it drives the respectable man to the Christ who never harbored a grudge and who took the sentence of the men who did.

stations.verse: Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.
note: John says it as bluntly as it can be said. Hatred is murder. Not like murder, not a step toward murder — it is murder, in God’s reckoning. This closes every loophole the respectable heart tries to open. A man cannot hold hatred in his chest and call himself innocent of the sixth commandment. John forces the issue: the disposition is the deed, before God. And that leaves every hating man in need of exactly one thing — the mercy of the One he hated last.
stations.question: Is there someone you would honestly say you hate — or have hated? Can you receive John’s hard word not as condemnation that crushes, but as the truth that drives you to the mercy of Christ?
stations.gloss: to hate, to detest, to regard with active hostility
stations.live: Pray for the person you most resent by name every day this week. Ask for one specific good for them, even if your heart lags behind your words.
body: Not mere dislike but settled enmity — the heart’s hostility toward another person. John equates miseō with murder because in God’s sight the hostile heart has already done to the person what the murderer’s hand completes. In God’s reckoning, the hatred in your heart has already done what the murderer’s hand finishes. The dust lets a man carry miseō — settled hostility — while feeling law-abiding. John collapses the distinction: hatred is murder before God. The only escape is not self-defense but the blood of the Christ who was hated and killed, and who forgives the murderer of the heart.

stations.verse: and killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead, to which we are witnesses.
note: This is the gospel’s dark answer to the sixth commandment, and its glory. The Prince of life — the one perfectly innocent of all anger and hatred — was murdered. And God raised Him. Peter says humanity killed the very source of life, and that killing became the means of life for the killers. The innocent was taken so the guilty could live. The commandment against murder is answered by the murder of the sinless Son, whose death pays for the death-wish in every human heart.
stations.question: Can you see yourself among those for whom the innocent Christ was killed — the guilty going free because the Prince of life was taken? How does His death for murderers meet the contempt in your own heart?
stations.gloss: prince, founder, originator, pioneer; the source and leader of a thing
stations.live: Read Acts 3:12–19 this week and put yourself among the crowd Peter speaks to. Then hear verse 19 as spoken to you: “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out.”
body: Christ is the archēgos of life — its very Prince and origin. Humanity murdered the source of life itself, and in that death life was purchased for the murderers. They killed the Prince of life — and His death became the life of the ones who killed Him. The dust makes every man complicit in the death-wish that nailed the archēgos to a cross. And there the exchange is made: the Prince of life taken, so that men full of death could live. The commandment against murder is fulfilled by the murder that saves.

stations.verse: Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.” Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
note: This is what the Spirit produces in a man freed from the murder of contempt: not just the absence of hatred, but active love toward the enemy. Paul takes the sixth commandment past “do not kill” all the way to “feed him.” This is the heart of Christ reproduced in a man — the same heart that prayed “Father, forgive them” from the cross. The death-wish is not merely suppressed; it is replaced, by the Spirit, with a wish for the enemy’s good.
stations.question: Toward the one you have held in contempt, what would “overcoming evil with good” look like — a concrete good you could actually do? How might the Spirit be inviting you to replace the death-wish with a life-wish?
stations.gloss: to conquer, to overcome, to be victorious
stations.live: Do one concrete good this week for someone who has wronged you — a meal, a kind word, a favor. Do it quietly. That is how evil is overcome.
body: Paul commands a strange conquest: overcome evil not by matching it but with good — nikaō the evil by refusing to return it and returning good instead. The victory is won by love, not by force. You do not defeat the enemy by out-hating him. You conquer the evil by overcoming it with good. The dust wants a man to nikaō his enemy by hatred, and calls it justice. The Spirit teaches a truer conquest: overcome evil with good, replace the death-wish with love, and win the victory Christ won from the cross — love for the ones who took His life.

practices.title: NAME THE FACE
practices.body: Name honestly the person you hold in contempt — the one whose downfall you would quietly enjoy. Do not soften it. Write: “Jesus calls the contempt in my heart toward them murder.” Let the commandment stop your self-righteous mouth and show you the death-wish you did not think you had.

practices.title: BRING THE CONTEMPT TO THE CROSS
practices.body: Take that contempt to the One who died for it. Pray: “Christ, You were murdered by men full of hatred — including me. Your death covers the murder in my heart. Drain it out.” Receive both His perfect love as your covering and His blood as your cleansing. Do not carry it alone.

practices.title: WISH ONE ENEMY LIFE
practices.body: Toward the person you have wished smaller, practice the opposite this week. Ask God to bless them — mean it as best you can. If you can, do one concrete good, however small. Practice letting the Spirit replace the death-wish with a life-wish, overcoming evil with good.

practices.title: MAKE THE PHONE CALL
practices.body: Jesus says if your brother has something against you, go first (Matthew 5:23–24). Name the man. Make the call, write the letter, or knock on the door this week. You are not responsible for his answer. You are responsible for going.

practices.title: WATCH YOUR MOUTH FOR ONE DAY
practices.body: For one full day, listen for contempt in your own speech — the eye-roll, the nickname, the “fool.” Each time you hear it, stop and pray silently for the person you just diminished.

title: You Shall Not Murder
subtitle: the anger beneath the act — and the Life that was taken so we could live

passage.text: “You shall not murder.
“You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’

But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna.
“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Agree with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way; lest perhaps the prosecutor deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison.
Most certainly I tell you, you shall by no means get out of there, until you have paid the last penny.

stationsIntro: The verses below move through the sixth commandment and out to the Scriptures that expose the murder in your anger and reveal the Life taken for you — the sanctity of the image, the anger Jesus calls murder, the hatred John calls murder, the Prince of life killed, and the love that overcomes. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread leads from the dust of your contempt to the Christ who died for men full of death.
lifeIntro: This week is about facing the murder in your own anger and receiving the Christ who died for men full of death. The point is not to suppress hatred by willpower, but to let it be named, brought to the cross, and replaced by the Spirit with love. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Father, I have kept my hands clean and my heart full of contempt. I have wished men smaller and enjoyed their trouble. Jesus calls that murder, and He is right. Thank You that the Prince of life was killed for men like me, and prayed for His killers while they did it. Drain the contempt out of me. Teach me to wish my enemy life. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have kept my hands clean and my heart full of contempt.
I have wished men smaller and enjoyed their trouble.
Jesus calls that murder, and He is right.
Thank You that the Prince of life was killed for men like me,
and prayed for His killers while they did it.
Drain the contempt out of me.
Teach me to wish my enemy life. Amen.
bottomLine: Behind every murder is anger, and behind the anger is contempt that wishes a man gone. Jesus traces the sixth commandment into your heart and finds it broken there. Then He answers it with His own death: the Prince of life killed so that the guilty could live, and rising to give them a heart that loves.
benediction: Brother, you read “you shall not murder” and relaxed — and then Jesus took those two words and put your name on them. Because behind the act is the anger, and behind the anger is the contempt, and behind the contempt is the quiet death-wish that would be glad to see a certain person gone. You would never lift a hand. But you have nursed the grudge, savored the downfall, reduced an image-bearer of God to their worst quality — and Jesus calls that the seed of murder, growing in a respectable heart that thought it was innocent. The commandment for killers turns out to have your name on it.

And no man keeps it in the heart — but One did. Christ never hated, never held a grudge, never wished a man gone; even toward His executioners His word was “Father, forgive them.” That flawless love is now credited to men whose hearts were full of the death-wish. But the gospel goes deeper: the commandment against murder was answered by a murder. The Prince of life, perfectly innocent, was taken by wicked hands and killed — so that the guilty could live. The innocent Christ was murdered for the murderers of the heart, and in His death the sentence over your contempt fell on Him.

So when the old contempt rises and a face comes to mind — and it will — lift up your eyes. Lift them off the enemy you have reduced and onto the Christ who prayed for His. Lift them off the grudge you have kept warm and onto the innocent Life that was taken so yours could be spared. Lift them off the death-wish in your chest and onto the Spirit who is draining it out and teaching you, slowly, to wish your enemy life.

You do not have to purge the hatred by willpower to be revived. You have to bring the murder in your heart to the One who was murdered for it, receive His perfect love as your covering, and let His Spirit replace the death-wish with His own love for enemies. The sixth commandment exposes the murderer in the respectable man — and hands him to the Christ who died for men full of death, and rose to give them a heart that loves.
closingVerse: The commandment against murder was answered by a murder: the Prince of life taken so the guilty could live. Bring the contempt in your heart to the One killed for it — and be given His love for enemies.
carry: Whose trouble would you secretly be glad to hear about?

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Soul Dust to Revival
pulls: Adultery is covenant-breaking — and the deepest covenant you broke was not with a spouse. It was with God, the faithful Husband every soul has betrayed.
paras: The seventh commandment guards the most intimate covenant two humans make — and, like the sixth, Jesus takes it straight past the act and into the heart. “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery;’ but I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart.” The commandment men most confidently think they have kept becomes, in Jesus’ hands, the one almost no man has.

Adultery is covenant-breaking. It is the betrayal of a promise, the tearing of a one-flesh bond, the theft of what belongs to another. And Jesus locates the root of that betrayal in the lustful look — the moment a man takes a person made in God’s image and reduces them to an object for his consumption. The act of adultery is only the visible fruit; the root is a heart that treats others as things to be used, a desire that has slipped its covenant banks. And by that measure, the commandment has caught nearly every man alive.

But this commandment carries something the others hint at and this one shouts: God describes His own relationship with His people as a marriage, and their sin as adultery against Him. The deepest breach is not merely between a man and his spouse — it is between the human soul and God, who is the faithful Husband every soul has betrayed. And that is where the gospel of this commandment blazes: Christ is the Bridegroom who kept faith when His bride did not, who loved an adulterous people to the death, and who by His Spirit makes unfaithful hearts faithful again.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Why This Command
paras: This week goes after the lust and covenant-breaking you have excused, and the Bridegroom who was faithful to an unfaithful people. A lot of men have kept the letter of this commandment — never physically unfaithful — while breaking it constantly in the heart: the lustful look, the private consumption of images, the reduction of persons to objects. And beneath all of it is a deeper unfaithfulness, toward God Himself. This week means to name both.

The goal is to let the seventh commandment expose the unfaithfulness in your heart — toward spouse and toward God — and to lift your eyes to Christ, the faithful Bridegroom. Every road runs to Christ, and this one runs to Him as the Husband who loved His adulterous bride to the cross, who cleanses her and presents her spotless, and who by His Spirit is making faithless men faithful. The commandment that condemns the adulterer is answered by a Bridegroom who took the adulterer’s shame and covered it with His own faithfulness.

Because faithfulness is the shape of God’s own love, and marriage was designed to picture it. When God wanted an image for His covenant devotion to His people, He chose marriage — a husband’s faithful, exclusive, self-giving love for one bride. So adultery is not merely a private wrong; it defaces a picture God painted of Himself. The seventh commandment matters because it guards that picture, and because the lust it forbids is the same disordered desire that turns a man away from God to a hundred substitutes. A man who cannot be faithful in his desires — who consumes persons, chases substitutes, breaks his covenants — mirrors, in the flesh, the spiritual adultery every human heart commits against its true Husband. This commandment reaches all the way down to a man’s capacity for faithful love.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Lust Turns Persons Into Things
pulls: You Know the Reduction
paras: Jesus takes adultery back to the lustful look, and the key is in what lust actually does. Lust is not the same as attraction, which is God-given and good in its place. Lust is the moment a man takes a person — an image-bearer of God, someone’s daughter, someone’s wife, a soul of infinite worth — and reduces them to a body to be consumed for his pleasure. It strips the person of their personhood and keeps only the parts he wants. That reduction is the essence of the sin, and it is why Jesus calls the look itself adultery: it has already done to the person, in the heart, what the act completes with the body.

This is why the private world of a man’s desires is not as private as he tells himself. Every image consumed, every person mentally undressed, every fantasy entertained is a rehearsal in treating human beings as objects — and a man cannot rehearse that in secret without becoming, over time, a man who sees people that way. The lust he thought was contained leaks into how he regards everyone.
