subtitle: the wanting that has no floor — and the contentment of Christ
keyVerse: You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.

passage.text: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”
But I rejoice in the Lord greatly, that now at length you have revived your thought for me; in which you did indeed take thought, but you lacked opportunity.
Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.
I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.
I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.

stationsIntro: The verses below move through the tenth commandment and out to the Scriptures that expose your covetous wanting and reveal the contentment of Christ — the command against coveting, the covetous root of all sin, the God who will never leave, the great gain, and the joy that satisfied Christ. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. This last commandment leads from the dust of your restless wanting to the Christ whose heart was content — and prepares you for the celebration to come.
lifeIntro: This week is about facing the covetous engine beneath your other sins and being taught contentment by the content Christ. The point is not to suppress desire by willpower, but to have restless wanting given a floor in the sufficiency of God. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Father, my wanting has no floor. I look at other men’s lives and ache to have them, and I am never satisfied with what You have given. Thank You that Christ was content in You, even to the cross. You have said You will never leave me. Let that be enough. Teach me, at His feet, to be content. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, my wanting has no floor.
I look at other men’s lives and ache to have them,
and I am never satisfied with what You have given.
Thank You that Christ was content in You, even to the cross.
You have said You will never leave me.
Let that be enough.
Teach me, at His feet, to be content. Amen.
bottomLine: Coveting is the wanting that has no floor — desire unhooked from gratitude, always reaching, never resting. It is the engine under every other sin, and no willpower can reach it. Christ’s heart was content in the Father, and His contentment is credited to you, while the God who will never leave you becomes the floor under your wanting.
benediction: Brother, you have come to the last commandment, and it is the one that has been under all the others the whole time. You shall not covet. It is the only command aimed entirely at the heart — no hands, no act, no court — and it exposes the engine running beneath every sin in this book: the restless, ungrateful wanting that never says enough. You may have managed clean hands on the other nine. But the tenth goes for the low hum of discontent, the endless reach, the ache at a neighbor’s good, the sense that what you have is not enough and what he has should be yours. And there, like Paul, you have no defense. The wanting has no floor.

And no man gives his own heart a floor — but One had one. Christ never coveted. He wanted only the Father’s will; He owned everything and resented nothing; He looked at no man’s life and ached to have it, because His desire was wholly satisfied in God. Even facing the cross, His content heart said, “not my will, but yours, be done.” That flawless contentment is now credited to restless men. And more than credited — it is spent for you: the joy set before Him, that moved Him to endure the cross, was your homecoming. His content heart bought a home for the discontent, and His Spirit is teaching covetous men, slowly, the contentment they could never manufacture.

So when the old reach returns and the ache says “not enough” — and it will — lift up your eyes. Lift them off the neighbor’s life you covet and onto the Christ who wanted only the Father. Lift them off the next thing you are sure will satisfy and onto the Savior whose contentment is credited to you. Lift them off the wanting that has no floor and onto the God who is enough — and let the Spirit teach you, at Christ’s feet, to say with Paul, “I have learned … to be content.”

You do not have to conquer your covetous heart by willpower to be revived. You have to bring the wanting with no floor to the Christ whose heart was content, receive His contentment as your covering, and let His Spirit give your restless desire a floor at last: the sufficiency of God Himself. The tenth commandment exposes the deepest dust of all — and hands the restless man to the content Christ, who is enough. And now, with the whole Law read, only one thing remains: to see it all kept, all paid, and to celebrate.
closingVerse: The wanting that had no floor is given one at last: the sufficiency of God. Christ’s content heart — the joy set before Him was your homecoming — bought contentment for the restless.
carry: What are you sure would finally make you content?

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Soul Dust to Revival
pulls: Every command you broke, He kept. Every sentence you earned, He paid. The Law kept in His life, its curse paid in His death — and both given to you. It is finished.
paras: You have come to the end of this study. And after ten weeks under the Ten Commandments, you could be forgiven for feeling only the weight of them: ten mirrors, each showing a different angle of your dust, ten plumb lines proving you out of true, ten commands you could not keep. If the study stopped there, it would leave every honest man crushed. But it does not stop there, because the commandments never did. Every one of them was an arrow, and this week you stand where all ten arrows land: at the feet of Christ. This week is for celebration.

Because here is what the whole Law was always heading toward. Jesus said He did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it — to keep it, complete it, fill it full. And He did. Every command you broke, He kept. No other gods — He served the Father alone. No coveting — His heart was content to the death. Honor, faithfulness, truth, rest, life, the Name — He fulfilled all ten, in thought, word, and deed, without a single lapse, across an entire human life. The Law demanded a perfect record, and for the first and only time in history, a man produced one. And then, staggeringly, He gave it away — to you.

And there is a second thing He did, just as glorious. The Law did not only demand perfect obedience; it pronounced a sentence on every failure to render it — a handwritten record standing against you. And Colossians says God has wiped out “the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.” The list of every commandment you broke, the whole indictment, He took and nailed to His cross, and it died there with Him. The Law kept, in His life. The Law’s sentence paid, in His death. Nothing left to earn. Nothing left to fear. This week you do the one thing left to do: celebrate.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Why End Here
paras: This week goes after joy — the celebration a man is finally free to have when he sees the whole Law kept for him and the whole debt paid. Ten weeks of the commandments have done their humbling work; this week is not for more humbling but for the gladness that honest humbling makes possible. A man who has felt the full weight of the Law and then sees Christ carry all of it is a man who can throw his head back and laugh with relief. That laughter is the goal.

The goal this week is to gather up all ten commandments and let them land as gospel: Christ has done it. Every road in this study ran to Christ, and here they all arrive together. The Law that closed your mouth hands you to the One who fulfilled it. The dust that clung to your soul is met by a Savior who kept every command and paid every debt. This is the feast at the end of the road. You came in clinging to the dust. You go out celebrating a finished salvation — and sent to carry the news to the next man in the dirt.

Because the Law was never meant to have the last word — Christ was. If this study ended with the tenth commandment, it would end with a man exposed and undone, which is the Law’s job but not its goal. The goal was always to drive a man to Christ, and a man driven to Christ does not stay in the dust; he ends at a feast. So the final week is not another mirror. It is the celebration every mirror was pointing toward — the whole Law kept, the whole debt cancelled. The capstone of the Ten Commandments is not a command. It is a cry from a cross: “It is finished.” And the only fitting response to a finished salvation is to celebrate it, and then to go and tell.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The Law Kept in His Life
pulls: The Record You Could Not Produce
paras: Stand back and look at what the Ten Commandments, taken together, actually required: a whole human life, lived from the heart, in perfect obedience to all ten at once, without a single failure, from birth to death. No man has ever come close. Every son of Adam has broken all of them, most of them many times a day, if Jesus’ heart-deep reading is right — and it is. The Law’s standard was flawless, lifelong obedience, and it was utterly out of reach.

And then came One who reached it. Trace the ten back through this study and watch Christ keep every one. He had no other gods; the Father alone was His. He carved no false image; He was the true image. He never misused the Name; He kept it holy. He is the Lord of the Sabbath and your rest. He honored His Father unto death and His mother from the cross. He never murdered, never hated, but loved His enemies. He never broke faith; He is the faithful Bridegroom. He never stole but gave everything away. He bore no false witness; He is the Truth. He never coveted; His heart was content in God. Ten for ten, across an entire life, in thought and word and deed — the perfect record the Law demanded and no one could produce. This is His active obedience, and here is the wonder of the gospel: it is credited to you. When the Father looks at the man in Christ, He sees this record — the whole Law kept — reckoned to a man who kept none of it. You are counted as having done what only Jesus did.

Think of what this means for a man exhausted by ten weeks of failing the commandments. You do not have to produce the record. It has been produced. The obedience the Law required has been rendered in full — not by you, and now credited to you as though it were. This is why the gospel is not “try harder to keep the Law.” It is “the Law has been kept, and its keeping is yours.” The pressure to assemble a passing record, which drove you your whole life, is over. Christ assembled it. You receive it. And the man who receives it can finally stop striving and start celebrating — because the exam he was failing has been passed in his name.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: The Debt Paid in His Death
paras: But the Law did two things, and Christ answered both. It demanded perfect obedience — which He rendered. And it pronounced a sentence on disobedience — a curse, a handwritten record standing against every lawbreaker. Even with Christ’s obedience credited to you, there remained the debt you had already run up: the mountain of broken commandments, the accumulated indictment, the sentence the Law justly pronounced over your dust. That, too, had to be dealt with. And on the cross, it was.

Colossians paints it in one picture: “You were dead through your trespasses … He made you alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.” Picture the entire list — every commandment you broke, every count of the indictment — nailed to the cross of Christ, dying there with Him. The sentence the Law pronounced over you fell on Him instead. And the same passage adds the triumph: “having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.” The cross was not Christ’s defeat but His triumph — the debt wiped out, the accusers silenced, the powers stripped. And then the cry that ends the Law and the dust together: “It is finished.” His obedience credited, the record wiped out — both halves of the Law fully answered, in the life and death of the Son. There is nothing left for you to keep, and nothing left for you to pay. There is only a feast to enter, a Savior to celebrate, and a next man in the dust to go and tell.

stations.verse: Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.
note: This verse unlocks the whole volume. Christ did not scrap the Law or lower its demands — He fulfilled it, kept it, filled it full. This is why the commandments still stand and still matter, and why they are no longer a threat to the man in Christ: their whole demand has been met by Him. The Law is not abolished; it is satisfied — and its satisfaction is credited to you.
stations.question: Have you thought of grace as God lowering the Law’s demands — or as Christ fully meeting them for you? How does “fulfilled, not abolished” change the way you hold the commandments now?
stations.gloss: to tear down, to destroy, to abolish
stations.live: Pick the commandment from this study you most feared. Write beside it: “Not torn down. Fulfilled for me.” Read it aloud before you sleep.
body: A builder’s word for taking a thing apart stone by stone — used of the temple that would be thrown down. Jesus says He did not come to katalyō the Law but to fulfill it. He did not demolish what God built. He finished it. Christ did not tear the Law down to your size. He filled it full and handed you the fullness. The dust either fears the Law as an unmet demand or wishes it were torn down. Christ does neither. He leaves it standing and meets its every demand — so the commandments stand, satisfied, no longer a threat but a joy.

stations.verse: If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him the same day; for he who is hanged is accursed of God. Don’t defile your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.
note: The Law pronounced a curse, and this verse names its most public form: “he who is hanged is accursed of God.” A man executed for his sin was hung on a tree for all to see. Paul quotes this very line in Galatians 3:13 to explain the cross: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us.” Jesus hung where the cursed hang. The sentence the Law justly pronounced over your dust fell on Him, so that the blessing He earned could fall on you.
stations.question: Can you receive that the curse the Law pronounced over your lawbreaking fell entirely on Christ? Where do you still live as if you were under a curse He has already borne?
stations.gloss: a curse
stations.live: When you feel cursed by your past this week, read Galatians 3:13 aloud and say: “He became the curse for me.”
body: From the root qālal, to be light, of little account — the opposite of kāḇēḏ, to be heavy and honored. Deuteronomy 21:23 says the man hung on a tree is “accursed of God,” a qəlālâ of God. The Law’s curse made a man weightless before God. Christ did not merely pity you under the curse. He hung where the cursed hang. The dust leaves a man under the Law’s qəlālâ, sentenced and made light. Christ became the curse — hung on the tree — to buy the cursed out, so that the man the Law made weightless is given the weight of glory.

stations.verse: Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity, and passes over the disobedience of the remnant of his heritage? He doesn’t retain his anger forever, because he delights in loving kindness. He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
note: Micah asks a question with no answer but praise: “Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity?” Then he describes what God does with the sins of His people: “He will tread our iniquities under foot; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.” Not filed. Not reduced. Thrown where no diver can bring them up. Paul gives the same picture from the cross: God has wiped out “the handwriting in ordinances which was against us,” nailing it to the cross. The record that stood against you is gone.
stations.question: Can you picture your specific sins — the commandments you have broken across this study — thrown into the depths of the sea? What would it mean to stop fishing them back up?
stations.gloss: to throw, to cast, to fling away
stations.live: Write down the sin that haunts you most. Read Micah 7:19 over it, then tear the paper up and throw it away.
body: A vigorous verb — Moses throwing down his staff, the brothers throwing Joseph into the pit, a man flinging away what he will not keep. Micah says God will šālaḵ His people’s sins into the depths of the sea. Your sins were not reduced or filed away. They were thrown where no one will bring them up. The dust keeps a man haunted by the record of what he has broken. Šālaḵ is the throw: God flings the sins into the deep, and nails the handwriting against you to the cross. The page is clean.

stations.verse: For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous.
note: One verse holds the whole exchange. “As through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous.” Adam’s disobedience ran down through every son of his. Christ’s obedience — ten for ten, across a whole life, all the way to the cross — runs the other direction, to everyone joined to Him by faith. You are not only forgiven for breaking the Law. You are counted as one who kept it, because the One you belong to did.
stations.question: Can you receive the full exchange — your sin His, His obedience yours? What would it mean to rest entirely in His record, not your own?
stations.gloss: obedience
stations.live: Go back through the ten commandments of this study. Under each write: “Christ obeyed this for me.” Read the whole page as one thing.
body: From the verb for listening under — hearing and doing. Romans 5:19 sets two men side by side: Adam’s disobedience and Christ’s hypakoē. Everything turns on which man you belong to. You are not merely forgiven for breaking the Law. In Christ, you are counted as one who kept it. The dust leaves a man with his own failed record and no way to mend it. Hypakoē is the record that saves him: the lifelong obedience of the Son, credited to the lawbreaker who belongs to Him — the whole volume’s end, and the reason to celebrate.

stations.verse: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.
note: And this is the final word — of the cross and of the Law. It is finished. The Law kept, the curse borne, the debt cancelled, the righteousness secured — all of it complete, nothing left to add, nothing left to pay. This is not a sigh of defeat but a shout of accomplishment: the work is done. The soul that clung to the dust across these twelve weeks is met, at the end, not by a demand but by a finished salvation. There is nothing to do but celebrate it — and go tell the next man in the dust.
stations.question: As you close this study, can you truly rest in “it is finished” — the Law kept and the debt paid, complete? And who is the next man in the dust that this finished gospel is now sending you to tell?
stations.gloss: to bring to an end, to finish, to complete, to carry out
stations.live: Name the man in your life still face-down in the dust. Before the week is out, tell him in your own words that it is finished — for him too.
body: On the cross it is tetelestai, “it is finished,” in the perfect tense — finished, with the results standing. The work of keeping the Law and paying its debt is tetelestai: done, and done for good. The whole Law kept, the whole debt paid — finished, and finished forever. The dust ends here, at tetelestai. The soul that clung to the dirt at the start of this study is met, at the end, by a finished salvation — the Law fulfilled, the debt paid, nothing left to earn or fear. There is only a feast to enter, a Savior to celebrate, and a next man face-down in the dust to go and tell that it is finished for him too.

practices.title: TRACE THE TEN, AND SEE THEM KEPT
practices.body: Sit somewhere quiet for forty-five minutes. Go back through the ten commandments of this study, and under each write two lines: “Here is how I broke it,” and “Here is how Christ kept it for me.” Then read the whole list as one thing: the entire Law broken by you, and kept, to the letter, by your Savior. Let it land as relief, and then as joy.

practices.title: CELEBRATE THE FINISHED WORK
practices.body: This week, do something a man does when a debt is cancelled and a victory is won: celebrate deliberately. Take communion if you can. Sing. Feast. Thank God out loud that it is finished — the Law kept in Christ’s life, the debt nailed to His cross, the record wiped clean. Do not rush past the joy. A finished salvation deserves a celebration.

practices.title: GO TELL THE NEXT MAN IN THE DUST
practices.body: Name one man still face-down in the dust — crushed by the Law, or blind to it, or exhausted by trying to keep it. This week, go to him, not as a man who kept the Law, but as one who could not and met a Christ who did. Tell him it is finished — for him too.

practices.title: REMEMBER TOGETHER
practices.body: Take the Lord’s Supper with your church this week if you can, and come to it on purpose. When the bread and cup are given, remember that the Law was kept in Christ’s life and the curse was borne in His death — and both are given to you.

practices.title: WRITE IT DOWN FOR THE NEXT MAN
practices.body: Write a one-page letter to a younger man — a son, a friend, a man in your church — telling him what you have learned in these twelve weeks about the Law and Christ. You don’t need to send it today. But write it as if you will.

title: It Is Finished
subtitle: the whole Law kept, the whole debt paid
keyVerse: Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.

passage.text: “Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.
For most certainly, I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not even one smallest letter or one tiny pen stroke shall in any way pass away from the law, until all things are accomplished.

Whoever, therefore, shall break one of these least commandments, and teach others to do so, shall be called least in the Kingdom of Heaven; but whoever shall do and teach them shall be called great in the Kingdom of Heaven.
For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, there is no way you will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.
You were dead through your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh. He made you alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses,
wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.
Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.

stationsIntro: The verses below gather the whole volume home — the Law fulfilled, the curse borne, the sins cast into the sea, the obedience credited, and the cry of a finished salvation. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. This last thread does not lead back to the dust. It leads out of it, to the feast, and then out the door to the next man in the dirt.
lifeIntro: This week closes the study, so the practices look back across all ten commandments, land in the celebration of a finished salvation, and turn outward to the next man in the dust. The point of Week Twelve is to celebrate and to go. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Father, I could not keep Your Law, and I could not pay what I owed. Christ kept every word in my place, and bore the curse on the tree. You have thrown my sins into the depths of the sea. Teach me to celebrate a finished salvation, and send me to the next man in the dust. Amen.

bottomLine: Every command you broke, Christ kept. Every curse you earned, He bore. The handwriting against you is nailed to the cross, and your sins are in the depths of the sea. There is nothing left to earn and nothing left to fear — only a finished salvation to celebrate, and a next man in the dust to go and tell.
benediction: Brother, you began this study face-down, your soul clinging to the dust, asking to be revived according to God’s word. And across twelve weeks you have been humbled all the way down by the Law of God — ten commandments that showed you, one after another, exactly how far your soul had fallen. If that were the end, it would be unbearable. But it was never the end. Every commandment was an arrow, and every arrow pointed here.

Because Christ did not come to destroy the Law but to fulfill it — and He did. Every command you broke, He kept: the Father alone His God, His heart content to the death, honor and faithfulness and truth and rest rendered in full, ten for ten across an entire life. That perfect obedience is credited to you. And the debt you had already run up — the whole indictment, the handwriting that stood against you — He took and nailed to His cross, where it was wiped out, and your sins were thrown into the depths of the sea. The Law kept in His life. The curse borne in His death. Your sin made His; His obedience made yours. And from the cross, the word that ends the Law and the dust together: it is finished.

So as this study closes, lift up your eyes. Lift them off the ten mirrors that showed you your dust and onto the Christ who kept every command they measured. Lift them off the handwriting that haunted you and onto the cross where it was nailed and wiped out. Lift them off your exhausting, failed attempt to assemble a passing record and onto the perfect one Christ assembled and handed you. Lift them onto the Savior who took a soul clinging to the dust and, by keeping the Law and bearing its curse, brought it all the way home.

You do not have to keep the Law to be revived — it has been kept. You do not have to pay the debt — it has been paid. There is nothing left but to celebrate a finished salvation, and then to walk out the door to the next man face-down in the dirt and tell him the same news: the Law is fulfilled, the debt is cancelled, the dust is not the end of the story. Christ has done it all. It is finished. Lift up your eyes — and go.
closingVerse: The Law kept in His life, the debt paid in His death, both given to you. There is nothing left to earn and nothing left to fear — only a finished salvation to celebrate, and a next man in the dust to go and tell. It is finished.
